study_subtitle: Concept Testing Report · Personal Finance MVP
single_sentence_takeaway: Pair real-time fraud alerts with shared partner tagging to cover the portfolio — but firm up fraud with a second round before committing the roadmap.
research_question: Which concepts most credibly serve customer needs for tracking recurring expenses, catching fraud, and sharing financial state with a partner?
method_description: Concept testing — past-use stories + per-need usefulness ratings
usage_guidance: Use for the MVP-scope conversation with product, design, and engineering leads. Each recommendation maps to a roadmap decision; treat sparse-coverage flags as a sequencing risk, not an indictment.

needs.statement: Track recurring expenses across all my accounts
needs.label: Track recurring expenses

needs.statement: Catch fraudulent or anomalous charges quickly
needs.label: Catch fraud quickly

needs.statement: Share day-to-day financial state with my partner
needs.label: Share with partner

top_findings.insight: No single concept covers the full need set; the portfolio only works as a pair.

evidence.metric: 0 of 3 concepts address ≥2 of 3 needs at high confidence

evidence.snippet: If you stick with the tagging it's the cleanest view possible.

top_findings.so_what: Building any one of these alone leaves at least two of three needs underserved — the MVP framing has to be a set, not a single winner.
top_findings.now_what: Plan the roadmap as a concept pair (most likely C3 + C2) and design the joint experience, not just the individual concepts.

top_findings.insight: Smart spend alerts (C3) is the strongest single concept — but the evidence is sparse.

evidence.snippet: Real-time alerts with context — that's exactly what fraud detection should feel like.

evidence.metric: n=3 of 5 (study ran out of time)

top_findings.so_what: C3 is the only concept that addresses fraud, and the same anomaly mechanism is a positive surprise on tracking — but the n is too thin to commit on alone.
top_findings.now_what: Run a focused second round bringing C3 to n=5 before locking it into the MVP.

top_findings.insight: Manual tagger (C2) owns partner sharing, but at a real adoption cost.

evidence.snippet: Same tags, same view, finally a way to align on what counts as 'eating out'.
Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money.

top_findings.so_what: C2 is the only concept that resolves shared categorization disputes — but tagging-as-mechanism is adoption-fragile and, for at least one participant, anxiety-inducing.
top_findings.now_what: Iterate C2 toward auto-suggested defaults with manual override, then re-test with anxiety-prone users specifically.

top_findings.insight: Automation with override is the design principle the data is asking for.

evidence.snippet: Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.

evidence.metric: Automation cited as up-driver on C1 (4) and C3 (3); manual effort cited as down-driver on C2 (4)

top_findings.so_what: Across concepts, automation drove ratings up; manual control was claimed in theory and rejected in practice. This is the dominant axis underneath the matrix.
top_findings.now_what: Make auto-behavior the default in every concept; reserve manual control for override, not setup.

top_findings.insight: Roommate-style sharing is an unmet need the portfolio doesn't see.

evidence.snippet: Honestly the thing I really need is a way to split rent and groceries with my roommates without a shared spreadsheet.
I want something for that — a way to set up shared recurring obligations with people who aren't my partner.

evidence.metric: 2 of 5 surfaced it unprompted; missed by C1, C2, C3

top_findings.so_what: Need 3 as scoped assumes a romantic-partnership context; 40% of participants surfaced a non-romantic-cohabitant variant. The portfolio doesn't address it, and demographic trends suggest the gap is widening.
top_findings.now_what: Scope a discovery study on roommate / non-romantic shared finance before the next concept round.

top_recommendations.insight: Advance Smart spend alerts (C3) — with a second-round fraud study before MVP commit.

evidence.metric: Only concept addressing Need 2 at high signal

top_recommendations.so_what: C3 is the most decision-relevant concept in the set, but the evidence base isn't yet wide enough to bet the MVP on.
top_recommendations.now_what: Run a focused C3 follow-up to n=5 within two weeks; commit to MVP only on confirmation.

top_recommendations.insight: Iterate Manual transaction tagger (C2) toward auto-suggested tagging with override.

evidence.snippet: Theoretically the cleanest. In practice I won't do it.

top_recommendations.so_what: C2's partner-sharing value is real and unique; its adoption-via-manual-tagging path is fragile. The fix is in the input design, not the value prop.
top_recommendations.now_what: Prototype auto-suggested categories with one-tap override and re-test, with explicit anxiety-prone recruit.

top_recommendations.insight: Re-scope Weekly auto-digest (C1) away from fraud; keep it as a low-effort recurring-expense surface.

evidence.snippet: A weekly email is way too late. Fraud needs to be in seconds, not days.

top_recommendations.so_what: C1 owns its target need (recurring expenses) at the lowest effort cost in the portfolio. Cadence makes it structurally wrong for fraud — don't fight the cadence; pair it.
top_recommendations.now_what: Drop C1's fraud framing; pair it with C3 (which absorbs the fraud signal in real time) in the MVP brief.

top_recommendations.insight: Commit to a C3 + C2 portfolio framing for the MVP roadmap discussion.
top_recommendations.so_what: Only this pair covers all three planned needs; C1 doesn't add coverage that C3 doesn't already provide.
top_recommendations.now_what: Frame the next leadership review as MVP = C3 + C2, with C1 as a candidate for a later release.

top_recommendations.insight: Open a discovery study on roommate / non-romantic shared finance.

evidence.metric: 2 of 5 surfaced unprompted; missed by all three concepts

top_recommendations.so_what: The portfolio as designed can't see this; demographic shifts make it likely to grow.
top_recommendations.now_what: Scope a 30-minute discovery study with 8 mixed-household participants in the next sprint.

concepts.name: Weekly auto-digest
concepts.description: A weekly email that automatically categorizes the past week's spending and shows changes from the prior week. No interaction required.

target_needs.hypothesis: Auto-categorization makes recurring spend visible without manual work
Weekly review surfaces anomalies the user might otherwise miss

concepts.high_level_finding: Low-effort pulse check on recurring spend, appreciated — but the wrong cadence for fraud.

recommendation.label: Advance
recommendation.rationale: Strong on its targeted need (recurring expenses) at the lowest effort cost in the portfolio. Re-scope away from fraud — pair with a real-time mechanism instead. Cadence is the structural cap.

concepts.name: Manual transaction tagger
concepts.description: Users tag every transaction with a custom category as it comes in. Tags are sharable with a partner who sees the same tagged feed.

target_needs.hypothesis: Manual control yields cleaner, user-defined categories
Shared tags align partners on what counts as what

concepts.high_level_finding: Owns partner sharing — at a real adoption cost.

recommendation.label: Iterate
recommendation.rationale: Owns partner-sharing — the only concept that does. But adoption fragility is real: 3/5 said they wouldn't tag, one experienced tagging as anxiety-inducing. Test whether shared tags can work with auto-suggested defaults and manual override.

concepts.name: Smart spend alerts
concepts.description: Real-time push notifications when an algorithm detects a transaction that looks unusual relative to your normal spend. User can dismiss, confirm-fraud, or mark-as-expected.

target_needs.hypothesis: Real-time anomaly detection catches fraud at the moment it happens

concepts.high_level_finding: Best single bet on fraud — evidence-sparse, but uniformly positive.

recommendation.label: Advance — with follow-up
recommendation.rationale: Strongest single concept in the portfolio: only one to address fraud, and a positive surprise on tracking. But evidence is sparse (n=3) and one participant's automation-distrust comment warrants probing. A second round to bring this to n=5 is the highest-leverage next study.

concepts.dist_note: Note: Sparse coverage (study ran out of time). All C3 verdicts carry medium-or-lower confidence as a result.

evidence.snippet: I would have loved this last month — I would've seen the Spotify thing immediately.
Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.

findings.notes: Strong consensus that auto-categorization is the key driver. P05 halo applied (see Methodology · Study observations) — does not undermine the verdict but does not strengthen it.

findings.reconciliation_note: Majority `partially` (3/5) with consistent explanations citing weekly cadence. P05 halo applied; P02's `not_at_all` reinforces the cadence concern. Held at `partial`.

evidence.snippet: It might catch some stuff but if I see fraud on Monday, this email doesn't help me until Friday.
A weekly email is way too late. Fraud needs to be in seconds, not days.

findings.notes: Cadence is the bottleneck. Concept was designed for fraud detection but the weekly delivery rhythm fundamentally limits effectiveness. Consider a real-time fallback for high-value anomalies.

findings.reconciliation_note: P05 halo applied. 4/5 explicit `not_at_all` with consistent explanations confirms the verdict.

evidence.snippet: This is just for me. My partner would never see it.
Email is one-way. There's no shared aspect to it.

findings.notes: Concept was not targeted at sharing and unanimously confirmed not to address it.

findings.reconciliation_note: Designed-vs-actual gap on adoption likelihood: ratings (2 completely, 3 partially) reflect that participants understand tagging would give the cleanest view, but most explicitly state they wouldn't actually do the tagging. P03's explanation cell was empty — flagged but does not change verdict.

evidence.snippet: If I'm tagging things anyway I'd put 'subscription' on the recurring ones — clearer than auto-categorization.
Theoretically the cleanest. In practice I won't do it.

findings.notes: The disconnect between theoretical and practical addressing is the dominant signal. C2 is designed for N1 but the manual-effort cost makes adoption fragile.

findings.reconciliation_note: Raw majority was `not_at_all` (4/5), which would normally yield `doesn't address`. P03's explanation explicitly describes the concept as anxiety-inducing — even one strong instance of the concept making the user's relationship to the need worse triggers `creates new problem` per the verdict rules. Confidence is low because the signal is from one participant; surfaced because creates-new-problem is reportable at any confidence.

evidence.snippet: Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money — I'd be anxious about getting it wrong, missing one, mis-tagging it.

findings.notes: Single strong signal — surfaced for further investigation. The risk is that tagging-as-mechanism, intended to give control, instead introduces money anxiety. Test in a follow-up study with anxiety-prone users specifically.

evidence.snippet: Same tags, same view, finally a way to align on what counts as 'eating out'.
If my roommate could see the same tags this would solve the entire shared-grocery argument.
We'd both see the same tagged feed — that's the whole solution.

findings.notes: C2 delivers on its target. The shared-tags mechanism resolves an explicit pain (categorization disputes) that participants had concrete past-use stories about. Note that P02's quote drifts toward roommates — see emergent need on C1 tab.

findings.reconciliation_note: n=3 (sparse) but 2 completely + 1 partially with consistent reasoning that 'an algorithm that knows your normal spend also knows your recurring stuff.' Not targeted, but the addresses verdict holds.

evidence.snippet: If you're catching every weird charge, you're also catching the recurring stuff that drifts.
If it knows your normal spending it knows your subscriptions, so why not.

findings.notes: Good surprise — C3 was designed only for fraud (Need 2) but the same anomaly-detection mechanism surfaces recurring-charge changes as a side effect.

findings.reconciliation_note: All 3 raters said `completely` with consistent positive reasoning around real-time + contextual content. Confidence is medium rather than high due to small n. P02's contradictory explanation is logged at study level (see Methodology · Study observations).

evidence.snippet: Real-time alerts with context — that's exactly what fraud detection should feel like.
Real-time and contextual — that's exactly the right shape.

findings.notes: C3 delivers on its single targeted need. The contextual alert content (showing what the charge is) was consistently called out as the differentiator from generic bank alerts.

findings.reconciliation_note: Only P01 rated this cell (1× not_at_all). Below the 2-participant threshold for actionable evidence.

evidence.snippet: It's a notification on my phone. My partner doesn't see my phone.

findings.notes: Direction is negative but the cell is structurally under-evidenced. Not actionable.

emergent_needs.label: Splitting recurring shared expenses with roommates
emergent_needs.confidence_note: Surfaced unprompted in 2/5 past-use stories (P02, P04); both returned to it spontaneously

evidence.snippet: Honestly the thing I really need is a way to split rent and groceries with my roommates without a shared spreadsheet.
I want something for that — a way to set up shared recurring obligations with people who aren't my partner.

emergent_needs.commentary: The "share with partner" need (Need 3) as scoped assumes a romantic-partnership context. 40% of participants surfaced a roommate / non-romantic-cohabitant need without prompting. The portfolio doesn't address it — and given the demographic shift toward later partnership, this gap may be larger than this study can size. Worth scoping a discovery study.

key_insights.lead_paragraph: Three concepts, read as a portfolio rather than as individuals — patterns of coverage, recurring drivers across the set, and a few design takeaways that don't fit a single concept.
key_insights.coverage_intro: Every need has at least one concept that addresses it, but each is owned by a single concept. There are no redundancies and one structural gap: no single concept handles fraud detection and partner sharing together.

coverage_by_need.summary: Well-covered. C1 owns it; C3 is a good surprise via anomaly-detection.
Single point of coverage. Only C3 actually solves it. C1's cadence is the cap; C2 makes things worse.
Single point of coverage. Only C2 — and its sharing value is yoked to a tagging behavior most users won't perform.

key_insights.coverage_so_what: Each need is held up by exactly one concept; two of three are single points of failure. C3 absorbs much of C1's value while C2 stands alone on sharing.
key_insights.coverage_now_what: Treat C3 + C2 as the MVP set and design the joint experience; do not ship any single concept on its own.
key_insights.drivers_intro: Aspects mentioned across multiple concepts reveal what the user population is actually responding to, beneath any single stimulus.

recurring_drivers.label: Contextual content (what the charge is, not just that one happened)

key_insights.drivers_so_what: The dominant signal is aversion to manual effort. Where automation worked, participants rated up; where the concept asked for input (C2), most said they'd rate it generously in theory but wouldn't follow through.
key_insights.drivers_now_what: Adopt "automation with override" as the cross-concept design principle going forward — auto by default, manual as escape hatch.

additional_insights.insight: Automation with override is the design principle the data is asking for.

evidence.snippet: Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.
Theoretically the cleanest. In practice I won't do it.

additional_insights.so_what: Across concepts, automation drove ratings up; the rare manual-control claim was rejected when participants thought concretely about behavior. This is the strongest design axis to extract.
additional_insights.now_what: Make automation the default in every next-round prototype; reserve manual control for override, not setup. Test whether C2's shared tags can ride on auto-suggested categories.

additional_insights.insight: C3 + C2 is the smallest concept set that covers the full plan.

evidence.metric: C3 covers Need 1 (surprise) + Need 2; C2 covers Need 3 — together they cover Needs 1, 2, 3

additional_insights.so_what: Building C1 alone leaves fraud and sharing unsolved. Building C3 alone leaves sharing unsolved. Only this pair has full plan coverage.
additional_insights.now_what: Frame the next leadership review as MVP = C3 + C2; treat C1 as a later-release candidate.

halo_participants.rationale: P05 rated completely across nearly every cell with vague, generic explanations ("sounds good", "this would help"). This is consistent with halo / acquiescence rather than considered judgment. Their ratings were down-weighted in every per-cell reconciliation. Treat P05's data as directional only — not as one of five equal data points.

sparse_coverage.rationale: C3 was rated by only 3 of 5 participants because the study ran out of time. This is why every C3 verdict carries medium-or-lower confidence even when the signal is uniformly positive. A follow-up round bringing C3 to n=5 is the cheapest way to firm up the strongest single concept in the portfolio.

contradictions.rationale: P02 rated C3 completely on fraud while saying "I don't really trust automated alerts" in the same breath. Logged as a known contradiction worth probing, not as an undermining signal — the rating itself was for the concept's shape, the comment was about a category-level skepticism.
contradictions.snippet: I don't really trust automated alerts. I always second-guess them.

study_setup.format: 60-minute moderated 1:1 sessions. Each session opened with a past-use story for each need, followed by stimulus-based concept presentation, followed by per-need ratings with explanations.
study_setup.sample: 5 participants, recruited for active personal-finance app use and at least one shared-spending context (partner or roommate). Mix of household structures.
study_setup.needs_tested: 3 functional outcomes from the team's job-map work.
